Nexperia previously called for talks in late November but saw no indication of willingness from Chinese operations.

On December 11, 2025, China’s commerce ministry urged the Dutch government to press Nexperia’s Netherlands arm to send personnel to China. Spokesman He Yadong asked the Dutch embassy to encourage the Nijmegen-based company to dispatch representatives “as soon as possible,” citing a need to “implement the consensus reached in consultations.” Wingtech, Nexperia’s Chinese owner, had invited the subsidiary’s independent directors and equity trustee to discuss corporate control and restoring global supply-chain stability. The ministry called the invitation a “positive development” and a show of “good faith,” noting Beijing facilitated negotiations. The request follows weeks of public disagreement between the two companies over willingness to talk.

The Chinese unit of Netherlands-based Nexperia secured silicon wafer supplies from local firms for all its 2026 IGBT production, after the Dutch parent suspended wafer shipments in late October 2025 amid a corporate dispute. The unit declared independence two months ago. The Dutch government took control of Nexperia from Chinese parent Wingtech in September 2025. Beijing halted exports of Nexperia’s finished products, triggering chip shortages for global automakers. Both governments relaxed measures last month. Wafer inventory in Dongguan is low, causing chip shortages for Chinese automakers and Honda, which suspended some China and Japan factory operations. Local suppliers include Wingsky Semi, Shanghai GAT Semiconductor, and United Nova Technology Co.

On December 22, 2025, Wingtech Technology co-chairwoman Ruby Yang warned that global chip supplies remain at risk unless control over Dutch chipmaker Nexperia is restored. The dispute, which became public in October, stems from a court decision suspending Wingtech’s founder as Nexperia CEO and placing shareholder rights under trustees. Nexperia’s Dutch entity halted wafer supplies to its Chinese facility, effectively splitting operations into two entities. Honda Motor Co planned production halts due to shortages. Yang accused the Dutch government of breaching a bilateral investment treaty, while Nexperia rejected allegations of executive self-dealing. The Chinese unit seeks alternative wafer sources; the Dutch side expands Malaysia finishing capacity. Wingtech may seek international arbitration.

Wingtech Technology Chairwoman Ruby Yang warned on December 23, 2025, that global chip supplies will worsen unless control over Dutch chipmaker Nexperia BV is restored. The dispute, which escalated in October, stems from a Dutch court decision suspending Wingtech’s shareholder rights and placing Nexperia under court-appointed trustees. Yang accused the Dutch government of breaching a bilateral investment treaty and local managers of seeking personal gain. The crisis has split Nexperia into two parallel entities: Dutch operations halted wafer supplies to the Chinese facility, while China-based operations sought alternative sources. Honda Motor Co. warned of production halts due to shortages. First talks occurred in mid-December, with Wingtech appealing to the Dutch Supreme Court and threatening international arbitration within six months, seeking damages including Nexperia’s estimated $8 billion value.

Nexperia China, a unit of Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and owned by Wingtech Technology, is seeking new domestic wafer suppliers within six months, with validation expected between Q1 and Q2 2026. The Dutch head office suspended wafer supply to the Dongguan plant on October 29 after Nexperia China refused payments, citing restricted fund disbursements. Despite a significant wafer supply gap, Nexperia China produced and delivered over 11 billion chips since mid-October, a 14% decline from its pre-dispute annual global output of over 110 billion units. The Dongguan facility, accounting for 70% of Nexperia’s total output, continues operating. Direct talks between Nexperia’s head office and Wingtech began last week.

Nexperia China is validating new domestic wafer suppliers after its Dutch parent halted shipments on October 29, 2025, amid a legal dispute. Wingtech Technology, Nexperia China’s owner, expects qualification of 8-inch and 12-inch power semiconductor wafer suppliers by Q1–Q2 2026. The supply gap has caused production stoppages at automakers, including Honda plant halts in Mexico, U.S., and Canada since October 28, with further Japanese shutdowns scheduled for January 5–9, 2026. Despite the disruption, Nexperia China has delivered over 11 billion chips since mid-October, down 14% from pre-dispute output. The Dutch government seized temporary control of Nexperia on September 30 citing national security, and a court hearing is set for January 2026. Wingtech may pursue international arbitration seeking up to $8 billion.

On Dec. 23, 2025, China urged the Dutch government to immediately revoke its administrative order against Nexperia, a semiconductor manufacturer owned by Chinese Wingtech Technology. The Chinese Ministry of Commerce called the intervention an “inappropriate administrative intervention in corporate operations.” Beijing asked Amsterdam to create favorable conditions for company negotiations to restore global semiconductor supply chain stability. The Dutch government took control of Nexperia in late September under the Availability of Goods Act, citing concerns over technology transfer to Wingtech following U.S. warnings. Earlier, on Dec. 8, China and Germany discussed the case in Beijing.

On December 31, 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce demanded the Netherlands "immediately correct its mistake" and end "improper administrative interference" in Chinese-owned chipmaker Nexperia. The Netherlands issued a September order blocking Nexperia from major decisions without government approval, citing concerns about relocation of production to China and chip supply security. This followed U.S. warnings that Nexperia could face sanctions unless its Chinese CEO was replaced. The Dutch government later suspended the order after talks with Beijing, but a court ruling removing the CEO remains. China retaliated by blocking exports of finished chips from Nexperia's Chinese facilities, later exempting civilian-use chips due to supply-chain concerns. Japanese carmakers Honda and Nissan announced production cuts from chip shortages linked to the dispute.

A Dutch court will hear arguments on January 14 over a formal investigation into alleged mismanagement at chipmaker Nexperia. Preliminary decisions in early October suspended former CEO Zhang Xuezheng and transferred shares held by Chinese parent Wingtech to a Dutch lawyer. In September, the Dutch government briefly seized control of Nexperia before reversing. The dispute has disrupted supply of basic chips to the automotive industry, causing shortages. Nexperia stated that there were sound reasons to doubt the course of affairs and that an investigation should be ordered. Wingtech confirmed the hearing date. A court decision will follow at a date to be determined.

Nexperia’s China unit is seeking domestic silicon wafer suppliers and expanding local packaging operations to stabilize production after supply disruptions. Wafer deliveries from Nexperia Netherlands were halted in October 2025, following the Dutch government’s September decision to take control from Wingtech due to governance concerns. Beijing responded by restricting exports of Nexperia’s finished products, causing global automaker chip shortages, but lifted those curbs in November, when the Dutch government also paused its intervention. Securing local suppliers would allow continued chipmaking without Dutch shipments. However, legal disputes persist: Wingtech appealed to the Dutch Supreme Court in December, and a court hearing on alleged mismanagement is set for January 14, 2026.

Wingtech Technology, Chinese owner of Nexperia, is selecting local silicon wafer suppliers for its Netherlands-based unit and expanding domestic packaging capacity, according to a Caixin interview with chairwoman Ruby Yang Mu. Most selections are expected by Q1 2026. This follows a corporate dispute: the Dutch government took control of Nexperia in September, halted wafer supplies to the Chinese unit, and Beijing responded by halting exports of Nexperia’s finished products, causing global auto chip shortages. Both governments relaxed measures last month, but control battles continue. A Dutch court hearing over alleged mismanagement is set for January 14. Wingtech still seeks to regain control.

On September 30, 2026, the Dutch government seized control of Nexperia, citing fears of transferring operations and intellectual property to China, but later revoked the move. On October 7, the Amsterdam Enterprise Court suspended Wingtech founder Zhang Xuezheng as CEO and stripped Wingtech of control over Nexperia’s shares due to doubts about management. At a public hearing on January 14, judges heard arguments on whether to order a full investigation into mismanagement allegations by Nexperia’s European executives, or reverse earlier moves. Previously, judges cited Zhang’s potential conflict of interest—his Shanghai factory sells wafers to Nexperia—and failure to implement governance changes to avoid a US blacklist. Nexperia makes silicon wafers in Europe for packaging in China.

On January 15, 2026, a Dutch court heard arguments on ordering an investigation into Chinese-owned Nexperia, a chipmaker central to a semiconductor dispute. The Dutch state invoked a 1952 law in September to seize control; in October, the court suspended CEO Zhang Xuezheng (Wing). Nexperia’s lawyers accused parent company Wingtech of a “scorched earth” policy destabilizing the firm. Wingtech’s lawyer cited “mystery” around the intervention. Zhang did not attend due to personal toll. The court will rule within four weeks; an investigation would uphold October decisions, while no probe would void them. In late October, after Trump-Xi talks, China resumed chip exports and the Dutch government suspended its takeover. Political tensions eased, but the court’s decision remains pending.

Taiwanese power semiconductor firms reported mixed financial results for 2025, with performance diverging across the sector amid ongoing supply chain shifts. The varied outcomes reflect changing demand patterns, inventory adjustments, and geopolitical factors affecting the global semiconductor supply chain. Some companies exceeded expectations while others faced headwinds from shifting customer orders and logistics constraints. The results highlight the uneven impact of supply chain realignments on power semiconductor manufacturers in Taiwan, a key hub for the industry. No further details on specific companies or figures were available.

Wingtech Technology, Chinese owner of Dutch chipmaker Nexperia, expects a 2025 loss of 9–13.5 billion yuan ($1.3–$1.9 billion) due to the Dutch government’s takeover of the semiconductor firm. Wingtech’s authority over Nexperia has been “temporarily restricted” since the October 7 ruling of the Dutch Enterprise Chamber, despite the government’s November 19 suspension of its invocation of the Cold War-era Goods Availability Act. The projected loss exceeds Wingtech’s 2.83 billion yuan loss in 2024 and reverses its earlier 265% year-on-year net profit increase to 1.51 billion yuan in the first three quarters of 2025. Wingtech cited significant investment losses and asset impairments, warning that uncertainty persists over whether the semiconductor business can maintain its prior momentum.

On February 11, 2026, a Dutch court ordered a formal investigation into alleged mismanagement at Nexperia, the Dutch semiconductor company owned by China's Wingtech Technology. The Amsterdam Enterprise Chamber cited "valid reasons to doubt the sound policy and conduct of business," pointing to "negligent conduct involving a conflict of interest" by suspended Chinese CEO Zhang Xuezheng. The CEO, suspended in October 2025, allegedly changed strategy without board consultation, failed to honor agreements with Dutch authorities, and restricted European executives' authority. His suspension and temporary director appointments remain in effect during the probe, expected to take months. Nexperia is a focal point in geopolitical tensions over semiconductor supply chains, particularly affecting automotive manufacturing.

On February 12, 2026, a Dutch court ordered an investigation into mismanagement at chipmaker Nexperia, dealing a blow to Chinese parent Wingtech. The ruling allows the European management team, installed after a Dutch state intervention last year, to remain in place. The corporate standoff between Europe and China over Nexperia has escalated from boardrooms to Brussels and Beijing, and has disrupted global supplies of basic chips to the automotive industry.

On March 7, 2026, China’s commerce ministry warned of potential global chip shortages due to escalating conflicts between Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and its Chinese subsidiary. The dispute began when The Hague seized Nexperia from Chinese parent Wingtech, prompting Beijing’s October export controls on Nexperia chips—widely used in auto electronics—which disrupted global auto production. Although the shortage eased after negotiations, tensions increased. On March 6, Nexperia’s Chinese packaging arm accused the Dutch headquarters of disabling employee office accounts. Beijing stated this disrupted normal production and could trigger another semiconductor supply chain crisis, for which the Netherlands must bear responsibility. The Dutch entity did not deny the IT action but disputed claims of production impact. The Chinese subsidiary declared independence after Wingtech’s removal in September; both sides have traded accusations, and Dutch HQ suspended wafer supply to the Guangdong plant. Diplomatic mediation from Beijing, The Hague, and Brussels remains unsuccessful.

On March 8, 2026, China's commerce ministry warned of a potential global semiconductor supply chain crisis due to escalated conflict between Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and its Chinese subsidiary. The dispute intensified after Nexperia's Netherlands headquarters disabled office accounts for all employees in China, disrupting normal production at the subsidiary's Guangdong assembly and testing facility. Beijing blamed the Netherlands for provoking new conflicts and threatening global supply chains. The crisis began in October 2025 when The Hague seized Nexperia from its Chinese parent Wingtech, leading to Chinese export controls. Despite diplomatic efforts, the impasse persists, with headquarters suspending wafer supply to the Chinese plant and both sides accusing each other of bad faith.

On March 9, 2026, China's commerce ministry warned of a renewed global chip shortage after Nexperia's Dutch headquarters disabled IT accounts for all Chinese staff on March 3. Beijing stated the action "provoked new conflicts" and warned the Netherlands would bear "full responsibility" if shortages spread. Nexperia controls ~40% of the global transistor and diode market, supplying consumer electronics and automotive sectors. The dispute began in October 2024 when Dutch authorities seized Nexperia from Chinese parent Wingtech Technology. China retaliated with export controls, disrupting production at Honda, Nissan, Volkswagen, and Bosch. Nexperia did not deny disabling accounts but claimed no production impact; China's ministry rejected this. Supply chain analysts note qualifying an alternative wafer supplier could take six months. A Dutch Enterprise Chamber hearing on the control dispute was held January 14, with no resolution announced.

According to a Reuters report on March 9, Nexperia China has begun manufacturing several chip types also made by its Dutch parent, using 12-inch wafers not produced in Europe. This follows an escalation of a dispute that began in October 2025, when the Dutch government blocked Nexperia from shifting operations to China. The Chinese subsidiary then declared independence and wafer shipments from Europe were halted. The unit is now producing bipolar discrete devices, Schottky rectifiers, and electrostatic discharge components. On March 7, China's Ministry of Commerce warned the conflict could disrupt semiconductor supply chains after the Chinese packaging unit accused headquarters of disabling IT accounts. Nexperia rejected the claim, stating its Chinese management had taken unauthorized IT actions. Mediation efforts have failed.

On March 11, 2026, Nexperia China announced small-batch production of chips using 12-inch wafers, producing bipolar discrete devices, Schottky rectifiers, and electrostatic discharge protection devices. This deepens its split with the Dutch parent, which does not use 12-inch wafers. The likely supplier is WingSkySemi in Shanghai. The dispute began in October 2025 when the Dutch government took control of Nexperia from Wingtech and halted wafer shipments; Beijing restricted finished chip exports, forcing Honda to suspend production. Both governments partially relaxed measures in November, but legal proceedings continue. Nexperia China reports delivering over 11 billion chips to 800+ customers since mid-October.

On March 13, 2026, the dispute between Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and its Chinese parent Wingtech escalated. After the Dutch government seized control of Nexperia in October 2025 on security grounds, Beijing imposed export controls on Nexperia chips, disrupting carmakers. China’s commerce ministry accused Nexperia of disabling IT systems in China and warned of renewed semiconductor shortages. Concurrently, Nexperia’s Chinese subsidiary began producing its own power and protection chips using 12‑inch wafers—a capability the European operation lacks—reducing reliance on European supplies. Elsewhere, Japan set a target to increase domestic chip sales fivefold by 2040, and India planned new incentives for local mobile phone production.

On March 13, 2026, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen held his first call with Chinese counterpart Wang Yi since the Netherlands seized control of Nexperia, a Chinese-owned Netherlands-based chipmaker and electric-vehicle supply-chain component. In September 2025, Dutch authorities ousted Nexperia’s Chinese CEO Zhang Xuezheng—founder of parent company Wingtech Technology, blacklisted by the US—citing prevention of technology transfer to China. Beijing responded with swift countermeasures. The row remains unresolved, but during the call, Wang Yi said China appreciated “positive signals” from the Netherlands, indicating a pragmatic reset effort.

Nexperia China will soon achieve fully local chip production in the second half of 2026, according to company sources. Since October 2025, its Dutch headquarters suspended direct wafer supplies to the Chinese unit, citing restrictions after the Dutch government seized control of Nexperia in September. China retaliated with export controls but later allowed civilian exports. Nexperia China has shifted from global to domestic production, using domestically made wafers. Its Dongguan packaging factory currently operates at 60-70% capacity, aiming for 90% by Q2 2026. Future production will center on factories in Dongguan and Shanghai.

China has cleared the way for a visit by Dutch trade minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma by quietly removing long-held sanctions against him, according to sources. The visit is expected before summer 2026, though no date is fixed. If it occurs, Sjoerdsma—from the new Dutch government sworn in on February 23—would be the first minister from that cabinet to visit China, at a time when bilateral relations need attention amid discord over Nexperia and ASML. He first expressed intent to lead a trade mission during a meeting with China's commerce minister Wang Wentao on the sidelines of a WTO summit in Cameroon last month.

Chinese firm Wingtech demands €6.8 billion compensation from the Dutch state for intervening in its Nijmegen-based subsidiary Nexperia last year. Caretaker economic affairs minister Vincent Karremans invoked a 1952 law to place Nexperia under state supervision, claiming he was preventing production and expertise from moving to China. The Dutch company court suspended Nexperia’s CEO Zhang Xuezheng and placed Wingtech’s shares under administrative control. China retaliated with an export ban on chips to European customers, halting car production in Germany. Nexperia makes transistors used in cars, phones, and solar panels. Karremans later admitted he “could have handled things differently.” In February, the Court of Amsterdam upheld the suspension, citing “valid reasons to doubt” Nexperia’s conduct.

Wingtech Technology and its subsidiary filed a lawsuit in a Guangdong court on May 22, 2026, provisionally seeking 8 billion yuan ($1.18 billion) in damages from Nexperia B.V. and five other entities, alleging continued restrictions on its control over the Dutch chipmaker. The conflict had been largely frozen since late 2025 after China reduced Nexperia chip export controls in exchange for the Netherlands suspending its seizure of Nexperia from Wingtech. Wingtech's net loss widened to 8.7 billion yuan in 2025 due to the dispute. Nexperia expressed regret, urging dialogue. The suit invokes China’s anti-foreign sanctions law, citing discriminatory Dutch measures. Wingtech had previously sought up to $8 billion via international arbitration in January 2026.

Wingtech Technology (Shenzhen, China) sued Dutch chipmaker Nexperia and three executives under China’s anti-foreign sanctions law in a Guangdong court on 2026-05-22, demanding full control restoration and 8 billion yuan (US$1.17 billion) in compensation. The suit follows a September 2025 Dutch government order to remove Wingtech’s control of Nexperia; though suspended, a parallel Dutch court ruling still restricts Wingtech’s authority. Wingtech alleges the measures constitute discriminatory restrictions under Chinese law. Nexperia responded that it had repeatedly invited dialogue, stating the litigation does not show a constructive attitude. The dispute signals escalating legal and supply-chain tension over control of a key doped electronic materials (HS4 3818) supplier.

On May 22, 2026, Wingtech sued Nexperia leadership in a Chinese court under China's Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law, arguing that a Dutch ministerial order from September 2025 and subsequent rulings constitute discriminatory measures. Wingtech demands reversal of Dutch governance measures, full ownership transfer of Nexperia B.V., and a provisional CNY 8 billion damages claim. The dispute escalated in October 2025 after Dutch intervention to prevent Nexperia's shift to China, leading to operational independence of Nexperia China and halted wafer shipments. In February 2026, an Amsterdam court ordered a governance investigation. Nexperia maintains supply continuity through alternative supply chains and is ramping non-Chinese capacity, expecting normalization in 2026. The lawsuit moves the conflict into China's legal system as a geopolitical dispute.

China’s market regulator SAMR fined Luxshare Precision Industry and Wingtech Technology for procedural violations in their now-collapsed asset sale, the latest sign of Beijing’s tightening merger enforcement. The deal, agreed in early 2025 at ~4.5bn yuan, saw Wingtech sell its assembly business (including Indian assets) to Luxshare amid US-sanctions pressure. Indian authorities seized the manufacturing assets on national-security grounds, leading Luxshare to seek Singapore arbitration in January 2026 to unwind the Indian portion; Wingtech counterclaimed. SAMR’s penalty, under the amended Anti-Monopoly Law, targets procedural lapses rather than competition issues, signaling to electronics groups that forced divestments under geopolitical stress will still face strict regulatory scrutiny.

On June 5, 2026, Chinese semiconductor firm Wingtech Technology filed a lawsuit against Nexperia Netherlands in the Dongguan Intermediate People’s Court. Wingtech seeks restoration of control over core assets and compensation, citing improper interference under China’s Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law. Nexperia China confirmed the filing, escalating a governance dispute that began after Dutch authorities intervened in late 2025, citing economic security concerns. The Dutch order was later suspended following talks, but tensions persist. Nexperia, acquired by Wingtech in 2019, produces semiconductors for automotive, consumer electronics, and industrial applications, with components widely used in European and Asian supply chains.
